Cyclone Kavira Disrupts Businesses and Transport Across Mauritius

PORT LOUIS, Mauritius, June 24 — Cyclone Kavira battered Mauritius for a second day on Monday, as sustained winds of up to 130 km/h and torrential rains brought widespread flooding, damaged infrastructure, and suspended most economic activity across the island nation.

The Mauritius Meteorological Services issued a Class IV cyclone warning late Sunday, advising residents to remain indoors as the storm moved slowly across the central plateau and northern districts. Authorities closed schools, government offices, and the main international airport until further notice. Sea ports suspended cargo and passenger operations, stranding several shipments and disrupting the supply chain for businesses.

Emergency services reported hundreds of calls overnight for flooded homes, downed power lines, and blocked roads, particularly in the capital Port Louis and the coastal towns of Grand Baie and Mahebourg. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Centre said at least 2,000 people had been evacuated from flood-prone areas since Sunday afternoon.

“The rainfall has been relentless, and some rivers have burst their banks,” said Jerome Bhugon, director of the centre. “Our teams are working around the clock, but conditions remain hazardous.”

Widespread power outages affected tens of thousands of customers, as the Central Electricity Board struggled to restore service amid the ongoing storm. Telecommunications companies reported spotty mobile and internet connectivity in several regions.

Economic activity across Mauritius ground to a near standstill. The Mauritius Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimated that retail and hospitality businesses in Port Louis and major tourist areas could lose millions of rupees in revenue for each day of closure. “This is peak season for our members, and the impact is significant, especially with the uncertainty about when operations can safely resume,” said Chamber president Marie-Laure Ng.

The Mauritius Exporters Association said port closures and flight cancellations had delayed exports of textiles, seafood, and sugar, with perishable goods at risk of spoilage. “We are coordinating with authorities to assess damage and plan for resumption of shipments once conditions permit,” said Ajay Koenig, the association’s vice-chair.

Analysts warned that the full economic toll would depend on the storm’s duration and the extent of infrastructure damage. “Mauritius is no stranger to cyclones, but Kavira’s slow movement and heavy rainfall pose a serious challenge,” said Ravina Bhookun, an economist at the Indian Ocean Policy Institute. “Recovery could take weeks, especially for small businesses and agriculture.”

No fatalities had been reported as of Monday evening, but officials urged continued caution. “The cyclone is still active, and the risk of landslides and additional flooding remains high,” Bhugon said. “We ask everyone to stay vigilant and follow official guidance.”
